issues.legal_issue: A buyer who fails to pay the balance of the price and complete a sale after the seller has performed or remained ready to perform the seller’s obligations commits the breach of the sale agreement.
material_facts: The seller delivered possession of the property agreed to be sold.
The buyer paid the amount due upon delivery of possession but did not pay the balance or obtain the conveyance by the agreed deadline.
The seller was willing to execute the conveyance, and the court found that the buyer’s claims about a shortfall in the land and additional oral terms were not established.
issues.conclusion: The buyer, rather than the seller, committed the breach of the contract.
issues.legal_principle: The court determines which party breached by assessing the written agreement, the parties’ conduct and the evidence of their performance; it found the seller had performed his obligation to put the buyer in possession and remained willing to convey, while the buyer failed to complete the purchase.

rule.if: sale_contract_dispute and seller_delivered_agreed_possession and seller_was_ready_to_convey and buyer_failed_to_pay_balance

predicates.sale_contract_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.seller_delivered_agreed_possession: The seller delivered possession of the property that the agreement required the seller to deliver.
predicates.seller_was_ready_to_convey: The seller remained willing to execute the conveyance required by the agreement.
predicates.buyer_failed_to_pay_balance: The buyer did not pay the balance of the agreed price.

issues.definition: When a sale-contract dispute involves delivery of the agreed possession and the seller’s readiness to convey, a buyer’s failure to pay the balance means the buyer committed the breach.

issues.legal_issue: A contractual term imposing forfeiture of money already paid as a penalty is subject to the court’s power to award only reasonable compensation, not exceeding the amount stipulated for forfeiture.
material_facts: The agreement expressly identified Rs. 1,000 as earnest money and provided for forfeiture of Rs. 25,000 if the buyer failed to complete the purchase.
The remaining Rs. 24,000 was paid out of the sale price when possession was delivered, not as earnest money.
The buyer committed the breach, but there was no proof that the property had depreciated or that the seller suffered other loss from the breach.
The seller retained the benefit of the Rs. 24,000 during the relevant period, and the seller’s loss from being kept out of possession was separately compensated through mesne profits.
issues.conclusion: The seller could retain the Rs. 1,000 paid as earnest money, but could not retain the remaining Rs. 24,000 or receive the additional damages awarded by the High Court; the earnest money and the benefit of retaining the remaining sum were sufficient compensation on the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 applies to every stipulation by way of penalty, including forfeiture of money already paid under a contract. It permits only reasonable compensation, capped by the amount stipulated, and does not permit compensation where no legal injury resulted. The court distinguished Abdul Gani & Co. v. Trustees of the Port of Bombay, I.L.R. 1952 Bom. 747, and Natesa Aiyar v. Appavu Padayachi, (1913) I.L.R. 38 Mad. 178, insofar as they treated forfeiture of an amount already paid as outside section 74.

predicates.contract_breach_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim arising from breach of a contract.
predicates.contract_stipulates_forfeiture_of_money_: The contract provides that money already paid under it may be forfeited if a party defaults.
predicates.forfeiture_term_is_a_penalty: The forfeiture term imposes a penalty rather than identifying the forfeited money as earnest money.
predicates.no_proven_loss_beyond_compensated_posses: No loss beyond the loss of possession, which is separately compensated, is proved to have resulted from the breach.

issues.definition: If a contract-breach proceeding involves a penalty term forfeiting money already paid and no uncompensated loss is proved, the forfeiture is limited to reasonable compensation up to the stipulated amount.

issues.legal_issue: Mesne profits for wrongful possession are measured by the value of the property’s use to the person in wrongful possession and include interest on those profits.
material_facts: After the sale agreement fell through, the buyer remained in possession and was liable to compensate the seller for that possession.
The trial court fixed monthly mesne profits at Rs. 140, while the High Court used a percentage of its estimate of the property’s value to award a higher amount.
The record did not establish the property’s standard rent, and the evidence did not justify the High Court’s method of estimating compensation from the property’s capital value.
The seller had separately claimed mesne profits, and the trial court’s monthly rate was not shown to be excessive.
issues.conclusion: The seller was entitled to mesne profits at Rs. 140 per month, together with interest at six per cent on each monthly amount as it accrued, from the specified start date until delivery of possession, subject to the applicable limit on future mesne profits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(12) of the Code of Civil Procedure defines mesne profits to include profits actually received or which could with ordinary diligence have been received by a person in wrongful possession, together with interest on those profits. Their normal measure is the value of the use of the property to the person in wrongful possession, not an estimated return on the property’s capital value. Order 20 rule 12(1)(c) of the Code governs the award of future mesne profits.

predicates.mesne_profits_proceeding: The proceeding includes a claim for mesne profits for possession of property.
predicates.defendant_wrongfully_possessed_property: The defendant retained possession of the property wrongfully.
predicates.possession_followed_failed_transaction: The wrongful possession continued after the transaction giving rise to the defendant’s possession had failed.

issues.definition: When a mesne-profits proceeding concerns wrongful possession continuing after a failed transaction, the profits are measured by the value of the use of the property and include interest.
